items: Map your plateau into one of four categories (metabolic adaptation, water retention shift, hormonal fluctuation, or activity decrease) before taking any action, because treating all plateaus identically can extend ones that would otherwise resolve on their own.
Review recent sodium intake, restaurant meals, and carbohydrate changes that could be causing a water retention shift plateau, because hidden water weight often masks actual fat loss underneath.

Consider hormonal factors if you have a menstrual cycle and have been plateaued for 10-14 days, because the menstrual cycle causes predictable water retention and appetite changes that stall weight loss for 1-2 weeks per cycle.

Check your daily step count and movement patterns over the past month, because NEAT (non-exercise activity) often drops gradually without awareness and decreases your calorie burn without any change in formal exercise.

Weigh yourself daily and track small fluctuations of 0.5-2 pounds, because frequent small swings indicate water weight changes rather than true fat loss stalls, and this distinction prevents unnecessary panic or intervention.

Track food and beverages consistently by weighing and logging everything daily, because inconsistent tracking often masks hidden calories that perpetuate plateaus and prevents you from recognizing real patterns.

Understand your expected plateau duration based on your specific type, with most lasting 2-4 weeks and hormonal shifts lasting 1-2 weeks per cycle, because setting realistic timeframes prevents the spiral of doubt that leads to abandoning your progress.

Use your plateau profile to distinguish between water retention fluctuations (which will resolve with continued tracking) and true metabolic adaptation (which requires recalculating your deficit or adjusting activity to break through).

If your plateau profile shows metabolic adaptation after 16+ weeks in deficit, hold your deficit steady and trust the process, because adaptation is a sign of success indicating your body has successfully adjusted—not a system failure requiring panic.

Wait through water retention plateaus without changing anything, because your body often releases retained water suddenly in a woosh moment, and consistent habits during this phase are essential for capturing that drop.

Make a change only when your plateau profile indicates a true metabolic adaptation plateau or your stall exceeds your expected duration range, because premature adjustments can reset your adaptation progress and extend the overall timeline.

Recognize that most plateaus resolve on their own with sustained consistency, because understanding this shifts your role from fixer to observer, which reduces anxiety and prevents counterproductive behavior changes.
